# Where we left off — Lecture 19

- Plotted body mass by species; Gentoo high, Adelie and Chinstrap nearly level
- `mass_model <- lm(body_mass_g ~ species, data = penguins_df)`
- `Anova(mass_model)` → **F(2, 339) = 343.6, *p* < 0.001**
- Reported: *"Body mass differed significantly among the three species."*

::: callout-important
**We skipped a step on purpose.**

We read that *p*-value without checking whether the model was allowed to give
it to us, and we never found out **which** species differ. Those are today's
two sets.
:::

# Goals for today

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
**Set 2 — the assumptions**

- Normality of the **residuals** — `plot(model)`, QQ, Shapiro-Wilk
- **Equal variance** — Levene's test

**Set 3 — the follow-up tests**

- *Which* groups differ — `emmeans` pairwise, Tukey-adjusted

```{r load-libs-16}
# Load packages at the top — always -------------------
library(tidyverse)      # wrangling + ggplot2
library(palmerpenguins) # the penguins data
library(car)            # leveneTest(), Anova()
library(emmeans)        # pairwise follow-up tests
```

```{r refit-16}
# The same data and model as Lecture 19 ---------------
penguins_df <- penguins %>%
  drop_na(body_mass_g, species)

mass_model <- lm(body_mass_g ~ species, data = penguins_df)
```
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
Every script starts from the raw data. Nothing today depends on objects left
over in last lecture's session.

::: callout-tip
`library(palmerpenguins)` again — base R has its own `penguins` with
`body_mass` instead of `body_mass_g`.
:::
::::
:::::

# 🧩 Set 2 · The Assumptions

**What a one-way ANOVA assumes:**

1.  **Independent** observations — a design question, not a test
2.  The **residuals** are normally distributed
3.  The groups have **equal variance** (homoscedasticity)

::: callout-note
Assumption 1 is about how the data were collected — no R function can rescue
it. 2 and 3 we can look at directly, and that is what the next few slides do.
:::

# Normality Is About the *Residuals*

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
A **residual** is one bird's miss: its mass minus its species' mean.

$$\text{residual} = y_i - \bar{y}_{\text{group}}$$

ANOVA does **not** require the raw masses to be normal — pooled across three
species with different means they are not even supposed to be. It requires the
**misses** to be normal.
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
```{r resid-16}
# What the residuals look like ------------------------
head(residuals(mass_model), 4)
```

::: callout-important
Shapiro on the raw `body_mass_g` is a different, wrong test. Always
`residuals(model)`.
:::
::::
:::::

# Assumption 2 — `plot(model)`, the Same Four Panels

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r diagnostic-plots-16}
#| fig-format: png
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-alt: "Four base R diagnostic plots for the body mass by species linear model in a two by two grid: residuals versus fitted values showing three vertical stripes, a normal Q-Q plot whose points track the line closely, a scale-location plot, and residuals versus leverage."
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(mass_model)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```
::::

:::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-note
**🔮 Predict first:** with ~340 penguins, will the Q-Q panel track the line?
:::

- **Three vertical stripes** in panels 1 and 3 — a categorical X has only three
  fitted values. Normal, not a problem
- **Panel 2 (Normal Q-Q)** is the normality check
- Panels 1 & 3 show whether the **stripe heights** match — assumption 3 by eye
::::
:::::

# Normality — Shapiro-Wilk as the Backup

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r shapiro-16}
# Shapiro-Wilk on the RESIDUALS -----------------------
shapiro.test(residuals(mass_model))
```

**W = 0.992, *p* = 0.051** — just above 0.05.
::::

:::: {.column width="45%"}
- **H₀:** the residuals are normal
- *p* > 0.05 → no evidence against normality

::: callout-important
**Large-sample caution**

With ~340 birds Shapiro-Wilk flags *tiny* departures. A *p* of 0.051 is not
"barely passed" — it is "the test is so sensitive at this n that it is nearly
flagging a QQ plot that looks fine." Trust the **plot**, use the test as a
second opinion.
:::
::::
:::::

# Assumption 3 — Equal Variance by Eye First

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r sd-16}
# The spread of each group ----------------------------
penguins_df %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarize(n    = n(),
            mean = mean(body_mass_g),
            sd   = sd(body_mass_g))
```
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
- Adelie **459**, Chinstrap **384**, Gentoo **504**
- The biggest sd is about **1.3×** the smallest
- Combined with **unbalanced** n (151 / 68 / 123), that is the situation where
  unequal variance actually matters

::: callout-note
Rule of thumb: equal n makes ANOVA forgiving about unequal variance. Unequal n
does not.
:::
::::
:::::

# Equal Variance — Levene's Test

::: callout-note
**🔮 Predict first:** given those sds, will Levene's test call the variances
**equal** (*p* > 0.05) or **unequal**?
:::

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r levene-16}
# H0: all groups have equal variance ------------------
leveneTest(body_mass_g ~ species, data = penguins_df)
```
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
**F = 5.12, *p* = 0.0064**

*p* < 0.05 → **reject H₀** → the variances are **not** equal.

::: callout-important
So the classic ANOVA we ran last lecture has a **violated assumption**. This is
not a mistake in the slides — it is what this data set does. Real data does
this constantly.
:::
::::
:::::

# When Equal Variance Fails — Welch's ANOVA

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r welch-16}
# Does not assume equal variances ---------------------
oneway.test(body_mass_g ~ species,
            data = penguins_df,
            var.equal = FALSE)
```
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
- **F = 317.6**, num df 2, **denom df 189.5**, *p* < 0.001
- Fractional denominator df is Welch's signature — it is the same correction as
  Welch's *t*-test, which is R's default `t.test()`

::: callout-note
**✅ The decision**

Levene says unequal → **report the Welch F**. The conclusion does not change
(both *p* are far below 0.001) but the *honest* test is the Welch one.
:::
::::
:::::

# A Decision Table You Can Keep

| Check | Result here | What it means | What to run |
|----------------|--------------|---------------------|---------------|
| QQ + Shapiro | *p* = 0.051, plot fine | residuals ~normal | fine either way |
| Levene | *p* = 0.0064 | variances **unequal** | `oneway.test(var.equal = FALSE)` |
| Both fail badly | — | normality **and** variance gone | Kruskal-Wallis (rank-based) |

: {tbl-colwidths="[18,22,30,30]"}

::: callout-tip
**For reference only — you do not run this today.** The rank-based backup is
`kruskal.test(body_mass_g ~ species, data = penguins_df)`
→ χ² = 217.6, df = 2, *p* < 0.001. Same answer again. When three different
tests agree, you can stop worrying about which one you picked.
:::

# What *Would* Change the Answer?

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
Here all three tests say *p* < 0.001, so the violated assumption cost us
nothing.

That is **not** a reason to skip the check. Unequal variance with unequal n can
push a *p*-value across 0.05 in either direction — you only know which case you
are in **after** you look.
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
::: callout-important
**The rule for this course**

Check → decide → test → report *the test you decided on*. Not "run everything
and report the smallest *p*."
:::
::::
:::::

# 🧩 Set 3 · Follow-Up Tests — *Which* Groups Differ?

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
The F-test said "at least one species differs." Look back at the boxplot:

- **Gentoo** is obviously above the others
- **Adelie and Chinstrap** sit almost on top of each other

A single *p* < 0.001 is perfectly consistent with *Gentoo differs, the other
two do not.* The F-test cannot tell those stories apart.
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
::: callout-note
**✅ Key idea**

A significant F licenses you to go looking. It does **not** tell you what you
will find.
:::
::::
:::::

# Why Not Just Run the Three t-Tests Now?

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
Because that is the problem we opened Lecture 19 with — three tests at α = 0.05
gives ~14% chance of a false positive.

A **post-hoc** (after-the-fact) test does the three comparisons **and** adjusts
the *p*-values so the family-wise error rate stays at 0.05.

The standard adjustment for all-pairs comparisons is **Tukey's HSD**.
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
::: callout-important
"Tukey-adjusted" means the *p*-values printed have **already** been corrected.
You compare them with 0.05 directly — you do **not** divide anything.
:::
::::
:::::

# Pairwise Comparisons with `emmeans`

::: callout-note
**🔮 Predict first:** will **all three** species differ from each other, or will
two be statistically tied?
:::

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r emmeans-16}
# Estimated means + every pairwise comparison ---------
mass_emm <- emmeans(mass_model, pairwise ~ species)

mass_emm$contrasts
```
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
**The answer:**

- Adelie – Chinstrap: 32 g, *p* = **0.88** → **not** different
- Adelie – Gentoo: −1375 g, *p* < 0.0001
- Chinstrap – Gentoo: −1343 g, *p* < 0.0001

::: callout-important
Two of the three species are **statistically indistinguishable** in mass.
"Significant ANOVA" never meant "everything differs."
:::
::::
:::::

# What `emmeans` Gives You

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r emmeans-means-16}
# The group means, with CIs ---------------------------
mass_emm$emmeans
```
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
- `emmean` — the model's estimate of each group mean
- `SE`, `df`, and a 95% **confidence interval**
- `emmeans(model, pairwise ~ species)` returns a **list** of two things:
  `$emmeans` (the means) and `$contrasts` (the comparisons)

::: callout-tip
`emmeans(model, ~ species)` with no `pairwise` gives just the means.
:::
::::
:::::

# Compact Letter Display — Who Shares a Letter?

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r cld-16}
# Groups sharing a letter are NOT different -----------
multcomp::cld(mass_emm$emmeans, Letters = letters)
```
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
**How to read letters:**

- Same letter → **not** significantly different
- Different letters → significantly different

Adelie **a**, Chinstrap **a**, Gentoo **b** — the pairwise table in one glance.
This is the notation you see over the bars in published figures.

::: callout-tip
Install once: `install.packages("multcomp")`
:::
::::
:::::

# The Backup That Matches Welch

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
Tukey through `emmeans` uses the model's **pooled** error — the thing Levene
told us to be careful about. The matching unequal-variance version:

```{r pairwise-welch-16}
# Non-pooled SD, Holm-adjusted ------------------------
pairwise.t.test(penguins_df$body_mass_g,
                penguins_df$species,
                pool.sd = FALSE)
```
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
- Adelie vs Chinstrap: *p* = **0.59** → still not different
- Everything else: *p* < 2e-16

::: callout-note
**✅ Same story.** The letters stand. When the robust version agrees with the
standard one, report the standard one and say you checked.
:::
::::
:::::

# Plot the Result — Means ± CI

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r emmeans-plot-16}
#| fig-format: png
#| fig-height: 2.7
#| fig-alt: "Estimated marginal mean body mass with 95 percent confidence interval error bars for each penguin species. Adelie and Chinstrap sit at about 3700 grams with overlapping intervals, while Gentoo is far above at about 5080 grams with no overlap."
mass_emm_plot <- as.data.frame(mass_emm$emmeans) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = emmean, color = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = lower.CL, ymax = upper.CL),
    width = 0.15, linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  labs(x = "Species", y = "Estimated mean mass (g)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

mass_emm_plot
```
::::

:::: {.column width="45%"}
- Adelie and Chinstrap intervals **overlap** — consistent with *p* = 0.88
- Gentoo's interval is nowhere near the other two

::: callout-important
Overlapping CIs are a **hint**, not a test. The *p*-value is the test; the plot
is how your reader sees it.
:::

This is the ANOVA cousin of the mean ± SE plot from the summary-stats lecture.
::::
:::::

# How to Report the Whole Thing

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
> *"Body mass differed among the three penguin species. Variances were unequal
> (Levene's test: F(2, 339) = 5.12, p = 0.006), so we report Welch's ANOVA:
> F(2, 189.5) = 317.6, p < 0.001. Tukey-adjusted pairwise comparisons showed
> that Gentoo penguins (5076 ± 42 g) were heavier than both Adelie (3701 ± 38 g,
> p < 0.001) and Chinstrap (3733 ± 56 g, p < 0.001), while Adelie and Chinstrap
> did not differ (p = 0.88)."*
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
**Every piece earns its place:**

- the assumption you checked, and what you did about it
- the test, **F**, **both df**, ***p***
- the follow-up, named as adjusted
- the **means ± SE**, so a reader can see the size of the effect
- the pair that did **not** differ — reporting that is not a failure, it is the
  finding
::::
:::::

::: callout-tip
Your Part B numbers will not match your neighbour's. One of the three columns

puts **Gentoo at the bottom**. Do not assume it will look like body mass.
:::

# What We Learned Today

::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
**Concepts:**

- Normality is about the **residuals**, not the raw data
- Unequal variance + unequal n is the case that actually matters → **Welch's
  ANOVA**
- A significant F licenses a **follow-up**; it does not name the groups
- **Tukey adjustment** keeps family-wise error at 0.05
- A shared letter means *not shown to be different* — not *proven the same*

**R skills:**

- `plot(model)`, `shapiro.test(residuals(model))`
- `leveneTest()`, `oneway.test(var.equal = FALSE)`
- `kruskal.test()` — know it exists; we do not run it today
- `emmeans(model, pairwise ~ group)`, `multcomp::cld()`
- `pairwise.t.test(pool.sd = FALSE)`
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
